subsystems.name: Tether ribbon
subsystems.role: the cable itself, running from the ground past geostationary orbit to a counterweight; it must carry its own weight plus climbers.
parts: protective coating against atomic oxygen and ultraviolet light

subsystems.name: Anchor and base station
subsystems.role: holds the ribbon down and lets climbers start their ascent.
parts: floating ocean platform near the equator

subsystems.name: Counterweight
subsystems.role: a mass beyond geostationary orbit that keeps the ribbon taut through centrifugal force.

subsystems.name: Climbers
subsystems.role: climbing vehicles that grip the ribbon and haul payloads upward.

subsystems.name: Power delivery
subsystems.role: climbers cannot carry enough energy for a 35,000 km climb, so power is beamed to them.
parts: high-power laser array at the base

subsystems.name: Tracking and debris avoidance
subsystems.role: nothing else can be allowed to cut the ribbon.
parts: small thrusters to shift the ribbon

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the fibre
buildSteps.detail: Individual carbon nanotubes, each only a few nanometres across but with near-perfect atomic bonds, are grown and spun into continuous yarn. This does not exist today at the required quality.

buildSteps.title: Weave the ribbon
buildSteps.detail: Yarn is braided into a wide, flat ribbon rather than a round cable, so small impacts damage only a few strands and the flaw can be inspected.

buildSteps.title: Deploy from orbit
buildSteps.detail: A spool of ribbon is launched to geostationary altitude and paid out downward toward the equator, while a counterweight moves outward to keep tension.

buildSteps.title: Capture the anchor
buildSteps.detail: The descending end is caught by a ship or platform at the equator and secured, completing the load path from ground to counterweight.

buildSteps.title: Install power and base infrastructure
buildSteps.detail: A laser array, tracking radar and payload handling facilities are built at the anchor station.

buildSteps.title: Fly the first climbers
buildSteps.detail: Uncrewed climbers ascend slowly with small payloads, stressing the ribbon and validating the grip and power systems.

buildSteps.title: Scale up traffic
buildSteps.detail: Once reliability is proven, climbers carry tonnes of cargo and eventually people, releasing payloads at geostationary or higher altitudes.

buildSteps.title: Add resource operations
buildSteps.detail: Payloads released at the top can be flung outward without rockets, supporting asteroid or lunar material transport.

prerequisites.why: the tether needs roughly 20–50 times the strength of steel per unit mass; today's best bulk nanotube yarns reach only a few gigapascals, far below what a self-supporting tether of this length requires.
climbers need hundreds of kilowatts delivered over long distances with good efficiency.

prerequisites.tech: Space debris tracking and collision avoidance
prerequisites.why: the ribbon crosses the most crowded orbits, where even a small fragment could sever it.
building and maintaining a station at geostationary altitude needs routine robotic construction in orbit.
the ribbon must survive decades of micrometeoroids, radiation and cyclic loading without failing.

pathway.unlocks: because the Moon's gravity is far weaker, existing high-strength fibres could work; this would move payloads from the lunar surface to orbit without rockets and build the operating experience needed for larger systems.

pathway.milestone: bulk nanotube yarn at tens of gigapascals
pathway.unlocks: laboratory-length ribbons strong enough to begin sub-scale tether experiments in orbit.

pathway.milestone: a full Earth-to-geostationary ribbon with robotic climbers
pathway.unlocks: very low-cost delivery of mass to high orbit and beyond, and routine handling of asteroid-derived material.
transport and resource extraction at a scale that chemical rockets cannot economically match.
